content: 1. Influenza is an acute respiratory viral infection caused by influenza viruses. Globally, annual seasonal influenza epidemics are estimated to result in approximately 1 billion clinical cases, 3 to 5 million cases of severe illness, and 290,000 to 650,000 deaths annually. In 2018, among children under 5 years of age, there were an estimated 109.5 million influenza virus episodes globally, with 870,000 hospital admissions and up to 34,800 influenza-associated deaths. 2. The burden of seasonal influenza epidemics in lowand middle-income countries (LMICs) is not fully understood, but research suggests that 99% of deaths in children under 5 years of age with influenza-related lower respiratory tract infections occur in LMICs. 3. There are four types of influenza viruses: A, B, C, and D. Seasonal influenza A and B viruses circulate among humans worldwide. Influenza C viruses are not typically captured by influenza surveillance, and influenza D viruses primarily affect cattle and are not known to cause illness in humans. 4. Influenza A viruses are further classified into subtypes based on the combinations of surface proteins, hemagglutinin (H) and neuraminidase (N). Influenza B viruses are not classified into subtypes but are divided into two lineages: B/Yamagata and B/Victoria. Only influenza A viruses are known to have caused pandemics. 5. As of March 2024, the influenza A viruses circulating in humans are subtype A(H1N1) and A(H3N2). The A(H1N1)pdm09 virus caused the 2009 pandemic and replaced the previous A(H1N1) virus. The A(H3N2) virus caused the 1968 pandemic and continues to circulate as a seasonal influenza A virus. 6. Seasonal influenza A and B viruses, as well as pandemic influenza A viruses, can spread readily from person to person via infectious respiratory particles (IRPs). These particles are expelled into the air when an infected person coughs or sneezes and can be deposited on the conjunctiva, mouth, nose, throat, or pharyngeal mucosa of another susceptible person. 7. The World Health Organization (WHO) defines modes of through-the-air transmission as either airborne transmission, where IRPs are inhaled into the respiratory tract, or direct deposition, where IRPs follow a short-range trajectory and directly deposit onto exposed facial mucosal surfaces (mouth, nose, or eyes). 8. Smaller IRPs may travel up to 2 meters. Additionally, influenza viruses can spread via contaminated hands or fomites, which are objects or surfaces contaminated with the virus, leading to inoculation into the upper respiratory tract. 9. Influenza pandemics can result in high illness attack rates, hospitalization rates, and mortality due to the lack of immunity in most of the global population to a novel pandemic influenza A virus. Hospitalization rates for children and non-elderly adults are often substantially higher during pandemic waves compared to seasonal influenza epidemics. 10. The effectiveness of antiviral treatment for patients with pandemic influenza depends on the susceptibility of the virus to these antivirals. If effective, the impact of antivirals in reducing the risk of hospitalization or death may be higher for pandemic influenza than for seasonal influenza due to the higher baseline risk of severe disease and death in untreated individuals. 11. It is critical to rapidly implement clinical trials during pandemics to assess the efficacy and safety of pharmacologic interventions. 12. Humans can sporadically be infected with novel influenza A viruses of animal origin (zoonotic influenza), such as avian influenza A subtypes A(H5N1), A(H5N6), A(H7N9), A(H7N7), and A(H9N2), as well as swine influenza A subtypes A(H1N1), A(H1N2), and A(H3N2). Human infections are primarily acquired through direct contact or close exposure to infected animals or contaminated environments. These viruses have not acquired the ability for sustained human-to-human transmission. 13. In their avian hosts, avian influenza A viruses are classified as highly pathogenic (HPAI), causing severe disease in birds, or low pathogenic (LPAI), causing mild or no illness in birds. Zoonotic influenza viruses associated with high mortality in humans include HPAI A(H5N1), HPAI A(H5N6), and both HPAI and LPAI A(H7N9). 14. Clinical diagnosis of influenza is challenging because the signs and symptoms can be non-specific and overlap with other respiratory pathogens. Reverse transcription polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR) is the gold standard for influenza diagnosis due to its high sensitivity and specificity. However, RT-PCR requires specialized equipment, and the turnaround time for results may not be timely enough for clinical decision-making. 15. Rapid diagnostic tests, such as rapid influenza diagnostic tests (RIDTs), digital immunoassays (DIAs), and rapid nucleic acid amplification tests (NAATs), are available in clinical settings and can provide results within 30 minutes. Proper specimen collection, storage, and transport are critical for diagnostic accuracy. 16. Nasopharyngeal or combined nasal and throat swabs are preferred for testing seasonal influenza A and B viruses or zoonotic influenza viruses in patients without respiratory failure. Lower respiratory tract specimens (e.g., endotracheal aspirate, bronchoalveolar lavage fluid) may be useful for testing critically ill patients with respiratory failure who test negative for influenza viruses in upper respiratory tract specimens. 17. Supportive and symptomatic care is essential for patients with influenza, as well as identifying those with severe disease or at high risk of developing severe disease. The clinical management of patients with severe influenza requires optimal supportive care, such as monitoring with pulse oximetry, providing medical oxygen, and respiratory support when indicated, alongside administering effective specific therapies for influenza. 18. Baloxavir, a newer antiviral with a different mechanism of action (selective inhibitor of influenza cap-dependent endonuclease) than neuraminidase inhibitors (NAIs), has been approved in some jurisdictions for early treatment of pediatric and adult patients with uncomplicated influenza. 19. NAIs, including inhaled laninamivir, oral oseltamivir, intravenous peramivir, and inhaled zanamivir, are widely available and active against all currently circulating seasonal influenza A and B viruses and zoonotic influenza A viruses. Oseltamivir is the most widely studied and available NAI. 20. The WHO guidelines present new recommendations based on systematic reviews of clinical trial data on the safety and efficacy of antiviral treatments and immunomodulators for patients with non-severe and severe influenza virus infection, as well as their use as prophylaxis in persons exposed to influenza virus.
